Then report the test score only from a split made after that step.

key=['pregnancies','glucose','blood_pressure','skin_thickness','insulin','age']

content.text:
The random forest gets **73.2% test accuracy** (90/123 correct on the held-out test set).

Before splitting, I removed 307 near-duplicate rows. The file has 921 rows, and many were altered copies of others: identical on the six integer measurements, with BMI and pedigree jittered slightly. All 307 matched a kept row with the same outcome, so I dropped them. That left 614 unique rows, which I split 80/20 stratified (491 train / 123 test, random_state=42). Without the dedup step, the test set could have contained near-copies of training rows, which would inflate the score.

The model is a `RandomForestClassifier` (500 trees, random_state=42) on the eight measurement columns. It reaches 100% on its training data, so it overfits, and the 73% test figure is the number to rely on.

Files written to `/home/daytona/workspace`:
- `train.csv` (491 rows) and `test.csv` (123 rows): the exact rows used, with all columns.
- `report.json`: test accuracy 0.7317, the model, and a note on the dedup step.
- `predictions.csv`: a `prediction` column with 154 rows (116 zeros, 38 ones), in holdout order.

I did not make any charts, so `live/` is still empty. I also did not retrain on train plus test for the holdout predictions, so those come from the 491-row model.
